name: Mahiyangana Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (hair relic stupa)
dynasty: Anuradhapura to Kandyan kings; modern rebuild
significance: One of the principal Buddhist pilgrimage sites of Sri Lanka, whose stupa is held to enshrine hair relics of the Buddha and was successively enlarged by rulers from Devanampiya Tissa and Dutthagamani through Vijayabahu I to Kirti Sri Rajasinha. The present casing over the older stupa was built between 1953 and 1980.
story: The Buddha is said to have come here in the ninth month after his enlightenment, subduing the yakshas who then inhabited the island and giving Saman a handful of his hair, which Saman enshrined in the first small stupa.

name: Seema Malaka
deity: Gautama Buddha (with subsidiary shrines to Guanyin, Kataragama deviyo, Upulvan and Ganesha)
significance: A meditation and ordination hall of the Gangaramaya temple, set on timber-decked platforms in Colombo's Beira Lake. The original late-19th-century pavilion was replaced in 1976 by a design from the architect Geoffrey Bawa, funded by S. H. Musaji and his wife in memory of their son, drawing on the forest-monastery layouts of Anuradhapura and Ritigala.

name: Warana Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (cave image house of Buddha statues)
significance: A terraced cave monastery on three levels whose foundation is attributed to King Devanampiya Tissa, holding Buddha images, wall paintings and a stupa on its middle terrace. Later kings including Valagamba, Nissanka Malla, Parakramabahu VI and Kirti Sri Rajasinha are recorded as renovating it.

name: Thuparamaya
deity: Gautama Buddha (right collar-bone relic)
significance: Regarded as the first stupa raised in Sri Lanka after the island's conversion to Buddhism, built by King Devanampiya Tissa at the request of the missionary Mahinda to enshrine the Buddha's right collar-bone. The dome standing today is the product of an 1842 rebuilding, ringed by the stone pillars of its former vatadage.

name: Sunandarama Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (image houses and a sacred Bodhi tree)
builtDisplay: Bodhi planted c. 1750; temple developed from 1970
significance: A Buddhist temple in the Galle District grown up around a Bodhi tree planted about 1750, with image houses holding Buddha statues including a marble figure presented from Burma. Its systematic development as a monastery began in 1970.
story: Its Bodhi tree is held to be one of the eight branches taken from the sacred Sri Maha Bodhi at Anuradhapura.

name: Kasagala Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (two ancient stupas and a Sri Maha Bodhi sapling)
significance: An ancient monastery in the Hambantota District whose origin is traced to the planting of one of the saplings of the sacred Sri Maha Bodhi, with construction generally credited to the reign of Kavan Tissa and later patronage from Dappula I, Vijayabahu I and Kirti Sri Rajasinha. Its two stupas are attributed to Devanampiya Tissa and Saddha Tissa, and its murals show southern Kandyan work with European decorative influence.
story: Local folklore derives the name from monks spreading their saffron robes to dry on the rock, which made the outcrop appear yellow from a distance.

name: Maligatenna Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (image house, stupa and Bodhi tree, with an old devalaya)
significance: A rock and cave temple in the Gampaha District with an image house, stupa, Bodhi tree and an old devalaya; an engraved stone door frame on the site has been assigned to about the 8th century. Its later history reaches into the Kotte kingdom under Don Juan Dharmapala and the Portuguese period.
story: Folklore holds that King Valagamba sheltered here during invasions and that the Buddha's tooth relic was hidden at the site for a time before being moved on.

name: Ovagiriya
deity: Gautama Buddha (granite image in the image house)
significance: An archaeological monastery site of about three hectares in the Ampara District, dated to the fifth century or earlier and formally identified by the Department of Archaeology in 1956. Its image house holds a 3.5 m granite Buddha, restored in 2008, and its stupa stands on an unusual octagonal platform rather than the customary circular or square one.

name: Samanabedda cave temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (image house)
significance: A cave temple near Uhana on the Ampara–Mahaoya road, traditionally attributed to King Saddha Tissa and now a protected archaeological monument. It retains a Buddha image in its image house and the remains of a ruined stupa.

name: Panasawanarama Purana Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (stupa, Bodhi tree and image house)
significance: An old Buddhist temple in the Gampaha District of Sri Lanka, recognised as an archaeological site, whose surviving elements are a stupa, a Bodhi tree and an image house.

name: Ancient Kadurugoda Viharaya
deity: Gautama Buddha (relic stupas; Buddha and Bodhisattva images)
builtDisplay: Anuradhapura period; dated pillar of Dappula IV (923–935)
style: Coral-stone stupas with fixed umbrella pinnacles
significance: A field of small grey coral-stone stupas at Kantharodai in the Jaffna peninsula, the most striking Buddhist archaeological site in northern Sri Lanka. Its history reaches back to the Anuradhapura era, a stone pillar there dates to the reign of Dappula IV, Polonnaruwa-period coins have been recovered, and finds include fragments of Buddha and Bodhisattva statues and Buddha footprint slabs.
story: The little stupas are said to hold the remains of sixty arhat monks who died together at the site, by poisoned mushroom curry or by famine, while fleeing persecution.

name: Naigala Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (Bodhi tree sapling, seven stupas and an image house)
significance: A monastery in the Hambantota District laid out on the Pabbata Vihara plan with panchayatana features and seven stupas, its founding credited to the kings Gotabhaya and Mahananga. Rock inscriptions at the site have been dated to the third to fifth centuries, and its Bodhi tree is counted a sapling of the Sri Maha Bodhi planted by an arahant.
story: King Mahananga is said to have been led by a great snake to a pool of water during a drought, and the place took the name Naigala, the rock the snake showed.

name: Kotte Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (reclining image; with a Kataragama devalaya)
style: Two-chamber image house with makara torana and Kandyan-era frescoes
significance: The royal temple of the Kotte kingdom, built beside his palace under the patronage of Parakramabahu VI, ruined in the Dutch period and re-established in 1818 after the site was rediscovered. Its two-chambered image house holds a reclining Buddha under Kandyan-era murals, and part of the old Kataragama devalaya survives alongside the stupa.

name: Ridi Viharaya
deity: Gautama Buddha (9 m recumbent Buddha and a gilded Anuradhapura-era image; also an Avalokiteshvara)
style: Cave temple with a Polonnaruwa-type gedige and Kandyan work
significance: The silver temple of Ridigama, founded in the second century BCE under Dutthagamani at the place where the silver ore that funded the Ruwanwelisaya is said to have been found. Its Rajatha Lena cave holds a nine-metre recumbent Buddha and a gilded Anuradhapura-period image, and the complex was revived in the eighteenth century by Kirti Sri Rajasinha of Kandy.
story: Merchants who had offered jackfruit to arhat monks were led to a seam of silver ore here, which provided the metal Dutthagamani needed to complete the Ruwanwelisaya stupa.

name: Sri Subodharama Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (image-house statues of 1780, a stupa, a Bodhi tree and a Sri Pada footprint shrine)
significance: A low-country temple at Karagampitiya whose vihara was finished in 1795 and its stupa in 1796, with Buddha images dating from 1780 and a Bodhi tree raised from the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi at Anuradhapura. Its murals are valued for bridging the conventional eighteenth-century hill-country manner and the more realistic nineteenth-century low-country style.

name: Neelagiriseya
deity: Gautama Buddha (relic casket enshrined in the stupa)
significance: A large ruined stupa at Lahugala set in a monastic complex of some 36 hectares, credited either to Kavan Tissa or to Bhatikabhaya. Excavation recovered a golden casket whose inscription led archaeologists to identify the contents as relics of the Buddha, and an inscription records a grant by Queen Chula Sivalee.

name: Padiyadora Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (torso Buddha image, dagoba and Bodhi tree)
significance: An ancient temple in the Ampara District whose construction is attributed to Kavan Tissa, prince of Ruhuna. Its remains include a dagoba and a four-foot Buddha torso, and it is still an active place of local veneration.
story: Its Bodhi tree is venerated as having grown from one of the saplings of the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi at Anuradhapura.

name: Gadaladeniya Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (seated image in dhyana mudra with four standing Buddhas; adjoining Vishnu devale)
style: Dravidian with Polonnaruwa-era Sinhalese and Indo-Chinese elements
significance: A stone temple of 1344 near Pilimathalawa, raised under Bhuvanekabahu IV of Gampola by the monk Seelavamsa Dharmakirti to a design by the South Indian architect Ganesvarachari. Its shrine holds a 2.43 m seated Buddha flanked by four standing figures, with a separate Vijayothpaya shrine of five stupas in cruciform arrangement.
story: The subsidiary Vijayothpaya shrine takes its name from the mythical palace of the god Indra.

name: Buddama Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (reclining image with several seated Buddhas)
builtDisplay: 3rd c. BCE; images of the Kandyan period
style: Cave temple with Kandyan murals and sculpture
significance: A cave temple in the Monaragala District said to have been built in the third century BCE and renovated by successive rulers from Udaya I and Parakramabahu I to the Kandyan kings. Its principal reclining Buddha is credited to Rajadhi Rajasinha and its walls carry Jataka scenes in the Kandyan manner.
story: Before Buddhism reached the island the site is said to have served as a training place for local craftsmen.

name: Trilokyanatha Temple
deity: Mahavira (with shrines to Lokanatha and Neminatha)
significance: A Digambara Jain temple at Thiruparthikundram near Kanchipuram, built in the reign of the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II and enlarged under the medieval Cholas and the Vijayanagara rulers. Its three parallel sanctums, entered through a three-tiered gopuram, centre on an image of Mahavira.
story: Local tradition credits its building to a Pallava follower of the sages Vamana and Mallisena, while another account attributes it to King Simhavishnu.

name: Mohankheda
deity: Rishabhanatha
significance: A Shvetambara Jain tirtha in the Dhar district of Madhya Pradesh, founded in 1884 by Acharya Rajendrasuri and dedicated to the first Tirthankara Rishabhanatha. It grew into a major pilgrimage centre around the acharya's memorial.
story: Acharya Rajendrasuri is said to have looked on the quiet land here and foretold that it would rise in holiness and become a great tirtha.

name: Mandaragiri
deity: Chandraprabha (with Parshvanatha and Suparshvanatha)
significance: A Digambara Jain hill temple complex near Madhugiri in the Tumkur district, dated to the twelfth century and dedicated to the Tirthankaras Chandraprabha, Parshvanatha and Suparshvanatha. A hilltop stupa there holds a stone slab carved with a footprint.

name: Ambapuram cave temple
deity: Parshvanatha and Mahavira (with an image of the goddess Ambika)
significance: A rock-cut Jain cave temple near Vijayawada, cut in the early seventh century during the reign of Kubja Vishnuvardhana, founder of the Eastern Chalukya line. It is dedicated to Parshvanatha and Mahavira and carries a relief of the yakshi Ambika, from whom the village takes its name.

name: Ahinsa Sthal
deity: Mahavira
significance: A modern Jain temple at Mehrauli in south Delhi, established in 1980 and dedicated to Mahavira, the twenty-fourth Tirthankara. Its large seated image of Mahavira on a low hillock makes it a well-known Jain landmark in the capital.

name: Arahanthgiri Jain Math
deity: Neminatha
significance: A Jain hill complex at Tirumalai in the Tiruvannamalai district whose principal 16-metre image of Neminatha is assigned to the twelfth century, with the ancient site now under the Archaeological Survey of India. A modern math was established beside it in August 1998.
story: The last Shrutakevali Bhadrabahu is said to have stayed on this hill with eight thousand ascetics to practise meditation and swadhyaya.

name: Shobhnath temple
deity: Sambhavanatha
builtDisplay: images of the 10th–11th c.; medieval dome
significance: A Jain temple within the ruins of Shravasti, dedicated to the third Tirthankara Sambhavanatha, whose recovered images have been dated to the tenth and eleventh centuries. An Irani-style dome was added in the medieval period, and Jain rulers are recorded in the area in the ninth and tenth centuries.
story: Sambhavanatha is held to have taken diksha in the nearby Sahetuk forest and to have spent fourteen years there before attaining moksha.

name: Muchhal Mahavir Temple
deity: Mahavira
significance: A Shvetambara Jain temple near Ghanerao in the Pali district of Rajasthan, built in the tenth century in the Nagara style. It takes its name, the moustached Mahavira, from the moustache shown on its principal image.
story: Rana Raj Singh I is said to have found a white hair on the idol's moustache; after the priest fasted three days the image revealed its moustache, which oozed milk when a hair was drawn, and the Rana became a devotee.
